40421.etyen:
Borrowed from German Nazi (“Nazi”), a colloquial clipping of Nationalsozialist (“National Socialist”), in this political use denoting a member or supporter of the National Socialist German Workers' Party. The German source word is formed from national (“national”) and Sozialist (“socialist”), whose elements ultimately continue Latin nātiō (“birth; people, nation”) and socius (“companion, ally”). First attested in 1931.

en.g: ditto, likewise; used as a response to indicate agreement or that what has just been said applies equally to the speaker
x: Jeg er glad i deg. — Ditto!
Jeg har savnet deg. — Ditto her. ― I've missed you. — Same here.
ditto her — same here; the same applies to me

1000421.etyen:
Borrowed from Italian ditto (“what has just been said”), an older regional variant of detto (“said; aforementioned”), the past participle of dire (“to say”). detto is inherited from Latin dictus (“said”), the past participle of dīcō (“to say, speak”), from Proto-Italic *deikō (“to show, indicate; say”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show, point out”). Doublet of diktum (“saying, statement”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ditto, Danish ditto, Swedish dito, Dutch dito, German dito, French dito and English ditto.

1000677.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Askeimr, a compound of askr (“ash tree”) and heimr (“home, homestead; farm”). The name originally belonged to a farm and was later transferred to the parish, town and municipality. The surname is habitational, from the same place or farm name.
First attested in 1337 in written sources, referring to the eastern Askim farm.
